Volume 08 · Chapter 07

Relative valuation and market evidence

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v08-c06

By the endUse comparable valuations with economically meaningful denominators and peer choices.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can construct a comparable-company valuation whose prices, claims, earnings periods and operating assumptions match; explain why an apparently low multiple may not signal a bargain; and reconcile relative pricing with a cash-flow valuation. Complete payout, liquidity and financial policy. Keep the claim and cash-flow boundaries of Chapter 2, the growth/reinvestment economics of Chapter 3, and the risk conventions of Chapter 4.

An analyst says that a component maker trades at less than five times earnings while its peers trade at seven. Before interpreting the gap, ask what “earnings” includes, which year's earnings appear below today's price, whether leases and outside shareholders enter the price, and how the peers were selected. Relative valuation uses prices as evidence. A precise division cannot make unlike businesses comparable or show that the entire peer group is correctly priced.

1. Define the claim before computing the multiple

A multiple divides a dated value by a specified financial or operating measure. In this chapter, E0 is the market value of parent ordinary equity immediately after date-0 distributions; EV0 is the value assigned to the specified operating business. B1 is normalized operating EBITDA for the next twelve months. A forward operating multiple is EV0/B1. It compares today's value with next-period annual earnings, not with a price expected one year from today. Multiples are conventionally quoted as “times”; switching an annual earnings denominator to a quarterly one changes the numerical multiple even if the business is unchanged.

Match value, earnings and the economic question
MeasureMatched constructionMain question or limitation
EV/EBITDAOperating EV divided by consolidated operating earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, with a stated lease basisHow much tax, maintenance, new investment and working capital stand between this subtotal and distributable cash?
EV/EBITSame operating perimeter divided by operating profit after D&A but before financing interestD&A partly reflects asset use; policies, asset age and acquisition accounting still differ, and D&A is not a maintenance-capex forecast.
P/EOrdinary-equity value divided by earnings attributable to that ordinary equity; price/EPS only with compatible share basesInterest, leverage, taxes, preference claims and outside ownership affect the earnings available to common shareholders.
EV/salesOperating EV divided by revenue of the same businessA revenue unit with a 2% sustainable margin is different from one with a 20% margin. Gross-versus-net revenue recognition also matters.
Price/bookCommon-equity market value divided by corresponding common book equityReturns on book equity, write-downs, repurchases and omitted intangible investment affect interpretation. Book value is not a liquidation guarantee.

Damodaran's definition and consistency tests motivate this claim matching. Dividing common-equity value by consolidated EBITDA combines a residual claim with earnings before other claimants are paid. EV/sales can be useful when earnings are temporarily negative, but it moves the problem into the assumptions about future margins and investment. For a financial intermediary, debt-like funding can be part of the operating business; an industrial EV/EBITDA template may then be inappropriate.

For a positive value, a negative earnings denominator gives a negative arithmetic ratio, not evidence of exceptional cheapness. At zero it is undefined; near zero, small measurement changes can generate enormous multiples. Keep such businesses in the candidate register and explain why a chosen positive-profit comparison does not rank them. If the target shares their failure risk, their exclusion cannot remove that risk from the target's valuation.

2. Reconstruct operating EV and the return to common equity

Under the capitalized-lease convention used below, define D as financial debt excluding leases, L as the lease-financing claim, P as preference claims, NCI as outside shareholders' interest in consolidated subsidiaries, C as separately valued excess cash, and H as holdings whose earnings are excluded from the operating denominator. All are date-0 values. Then

EV0 = E0 + D0 + L0 + P0 + NCI0 − C0 − H0;
E0 = EV0 − D0 − L0 − P0 − NCI0 + C0 + H0.

Consolidated EBITDA includes 100% of a controlled subsidiary's operating result. Parent common equity includes only the parent's equity interest, so add the market value of outside ownership when valuing the whole consolidated operation. Conversely, subtract a separately valued holding when its earnings are absent from the denominator. The primary source's enterprise-value definitions distinguish these two cases and explain why book NCI is an imperfect substitute. Debt also needs a dated market-value estimate; its face amount can be a poor proxy when rates or credit quality have changed.

Cash required to generate the modeled operations is not automatically “excess.” Restricted or costly-to-access funds need a supported value. Other obligations, such as a separately modeled pension deficit, enter only when their cash effects are excluded from the operating forecast; deducting both the obligation and its full future cash cost counts it twice. Options and other equity claims likewise require an explicit claim valuation or consistent dilution treatment, not a convenient share-count adjustment. The small lab stipulates no preference, pension, option or other omitted claim.

Lease convention. Our common denominator is before all lease payments, and our operating value includes L. All related productive assets, depreciation and renewal investment must be included when connecting this convention to DCF. An alternative after-rent convention leaves the lease payments in operating expense and excludes the corresponding financing claim. These conventions need not produce the same numerical EBITDA multiple. Mixing one convention's numerator with the other's denominator is the error. Real reports require a reconstruction of the actual asset, expense and obligation treatment; a reporting label alone does not establish it.

Worked example 1 — The missing claims in a quoted multiple

Fictional peer P1 has common equity 240 kCU, financial debt 80, lease claim 40, outside equity interest 20, excess cash 15 and an excluded holding 5. No preference or other claim exists. Its recurring annual operating EBITDA is 50 after the stipulated lease expense of 10, or 60 before it.

Capitalized-lease EV is 240+80+40+20−15−5 = 360, and EV/EBITDA is 360/60 = 6×. The after-rent operating value is 360−40 = 320, giving 320/50 = 6.4×. Those two complete conventions differ. Using 320/60 gives 5⅓×; using 360/50 gives 7.2×. Neither mixed construction answers the declared comparison.

If outside equity is recorded at book value 8 but worth 20, substituting 8 makes the capitalized EV 348 and the ratio 5.8×. Omitting both L and NCI gives 300/60 = 5×. No price fell in these calculations; the apparently lower ratio arose from omitted claims. Reversing the correct bridge returns ordinary equity 360−80−40−20+15+5 = 240.

3. Derive the multiple's economic drivers

A justified multiple is the ratio implied by stated cash-flow and discounting assumptions, distinct from a multiple observed in prices. Let next-year operating EBITDA be B1, D&A be dB1, and a fully usable operating cash-tax rate be τ. Under the clean stable model in Chapter 3, NOPAT1 = B1(1−d)(1−τ). If sustained growth g requires end-year net reinvestment g/R of NOPAT, where R is the relevant return on new investment and old earnings are maintained,

FCFF1 = B1(1−d)(1−τ)(1−g/R);
EV0/B1 = (1−d)(1−τ)(1−g/R)/(r−g).

This version assumes 0 ≤ d < 1, 0 ≤ τ < 1, R > 0, 0 ≤ g < r and g ≤ R; investment, earnings and the appropriate operating rate use the same currency, period and financing convention. Year-1 earnings are already supported by date-0 capital. Investment at the end of year 1 funds year 2, so the first numerator does not acquire free growth. Maintenance and renewal must be allowed for even when EBITDA itself adds back depreciation.

Holding B1, d, τ and R fixed, a higher r lowers the justified multiple. The growth derivative is (1−d)(1−τ)(1−r/R)/(r−g)²: more growth raises the ratio when R > r, is neutral when R = r and lowers it when R < r. Increasing the depreciation fraction while holding the other model inputs fixed lowers after-tax operating earnings; in an actual business, changes in depreciation can also signal changes in maintenance, asset measurement or capital productivity. EBITDA is therefore not a complete control for capital intensity.

Related identities expose other multiples: EV/EBIT = (1−τ)(1−g/R)/(r−g), and EV/sales equals EV/EBITDA times the EBITDA margin. For equity, a stable distributable fraction p of next-year common earnings gives E0/NI1 = p/(ke−ge) when the common-equity cash, financing and growth assumptions support that fraction. It is not valid to insert an operating reinvestment ratio into an equity payout formula without the financing bridge. These are conditional valuation identities, not evidence that every peer should trade at the same ratio.

Worked example 2 — Morrow's cash-supported multiple

Morrow Process Components is an original fictional case, separate from earlier chapters. All money is nominal kCU, all claim values are at T0 after distributions, and Y1 is the next twelve months. Normalized forward EBITDA is 50, D&A including leased assets 10, and sales 250. A fictional fully usable tax rate is 25%. Maintained returns on existing and new capital are 15%, stable growth 3% and the compatible supplied operating rate 9%. Replacement and new investment include the renewal of leased productive assets; no second lease payment, financing interest or tax shield is deducted or added in FCFF.

EBIT is 40 and NOPAT is 30. The reinvestment fraction is 0.03/0.15 = 20%, giving investment 6 and FCFF1 = 24. Opening productive capital is 30/0.15 = 200; closing capital is 206 and next NOPAT is 30.9. These assumptions support EV = 24/(0.09−0.03) = 400, EV/EBITDA = 8×, EV/EBIT = 10× and EV/sales = 1.6×.

Financial debt is 70, leases 30, NCI 10, excess cash 20 and excluded holdings 5. Net claims to remove are 70+30+10−20−5 = 85; common equity is 315. With 10 thousand ordinary shares, the conditional value is CU 31.5 per share. The 8× multiple summarizes the preceding cash model. It does not independently validate its 15% continuing return or its risk estimate.

4. Separate accounting adjustments, the cycle and the forecast

Write a bridge from the original reported measure to the measure used in comparison. First reconcile the reporting perimeter and lease convention. Next identify genuinely transitory costs and gains symmetrically. Then explain cycle normalization and the move from the trailing period to the forward period. A settled one-off cost removed from recurring earnings is different from a future cash obligation; the latter still needs to be paid or valued. A recurring cost cannot be made economically free by calling it unusual.

As a dated U.S. disclosure reference, SEC staff guidance inspected on 8 October 2026, with the cited general interpretations revised through 13 December 2022, identifies risks from excluding recurring operating costs, adjusting inconsistently across periods, or removing unusual costs while retaining unusual gains. It also distinguishes adjusted measures from its defined EBITDA and explains the net-income reconciliation. This is a scoped disclosure reference, not a universal accounting rule or a certification of the synthetic measures below. We call our denominator normalized operating EBITDA and specify every adjustment.

Stock compensation, recurring warranty expense, regular restructuring and ordinary customer-acquisition spending may be economically necessary even when noncash today or irregularly timed. Removing them needs an alternative cost, dilution or investment model; an unsupported addback is insufficient. In a real company packet, preserve the financial statements and the full reconciliation from net income as well as the analyst's normalization bridge. Our fictional input register begins at supplied management operating subtotals and does not claim to be a complete set of audited statements.

Cycle effects. At a cyclical peak, unusually high earnings can make a firm appear cheap; at a trough, the ratio can look expensive or become unusable. A normal earnings estimate needs a supported margin, capacity, commodity-price or utilization path. An average of past dollar earnings can misrepresent a company that has changed scale; a margin applied to comparable current capacity or sales may be more informative. Inflation, acquisitions and structural changes still need adjustment. Damodaran's normalization discussion distinguishes level and scaled approaches and highlights the timing of recovery. We do not assume that any fixed number of years establishes a representative cycle.

A normalized annual denominator is not necessarily next year's forecast. If recovery takes three years, label the denominator as a mid-cycle measure, use the same convention for peers, and model the transition in DCF. Do not replace all near-term cash by a recovered annual number. Similarly, a calendar-year forward estimate and a fiscal-year forward estimate can overlap different demand conditions. State the price timestamp, trailing endpoint, forecast window, forecast vintage, currency and information available at that timestamp; later restatements or forecasts must not leak into a historical comparison.

5. A complete candidate register and an auditable comparison

Choose the peer rule before examining which selection gives the preferred answer. Business exposure, customer concentration, pricing power, geography, cycle position, investment needs, growth, risk and accounting treatment matter. Industry membership supplies a starting universe, not proof of economic equivalence. A cross-industry peer can sometimes be informative if those drivers match; an industry peer with a different funding or failure model can be misleading.

The following entire fictional candidate universe contains six firms. The primary group uses industrial-component businesses with supported normalization and positive forward operating profit, matching Morrow's stipulated mature, positive-profit model. It does not use a price or multiple cutoff. P1–P4 qualify; P5 is a software-licensing business, and P6 is distressed with no supported positive normalization. Both remain visible. P6's experience remains relevant to an assessment of the target's downside. P4's high ratio remains visible despite differences in size and capacity growth.

Worked example 3 — Normalize six candidates, then price the target

All synthetic prices and market claim values are at the same T0; all forward measures cover the same Y1. Operating measures are fully consolidated. D excludes leases. C and H contain only assets excluded from the operating denominator; there are no other claims. The cycle changes are supplied conditional forecasts, not October 2026 observations. P4's added capacity was funded before T0; its forward depreciation includes that capacity.

P1 reconciles as 45+10+8−3 = 60. P2's 96 contains gain 6 and peak-cycle contribution 30, leaving 60. P3 reaches 30+8+4−2+10 = 50. P4 reaches 80 through its supplied forward capacity contribution. Their EV/normalized Y1 EBITDA ratios are therefore 6×, 8×, 6× and 9×. P5's 4× remains visible but belongs to a different operating model. P6's −18 arithmetic ratio is not ranked as a positive-profit multiple; the lab returns no meaningful ratio for its negative denominator.

The sorted included ratios are 6, 6, 8, 9. Their median is 7×; the equal-company arithmetic mean is 7.25×. The pooled ratio is (360+480+300+720)/(60+60+50+80) = 186/25 = 7.44×. It weights individual multiples by their earnings denominators: ΣEVi/ΣBi = Σ[Bi/ΣBj](EVi/Bi). It is neither an equal-company mean nor a market-capitalization-weighted mean. Positive denominators make those weights interpretable.

Applying the median to Morrow's matched Y1 EBITDA gives EV = 7×50 = 350, equity = 350−85 = 265 and CU 26.5 per share. The 6–9× observed peer span implies EV 300–450, equity 215–365 and CU 21.5–36.5 per share, conditional on applying those ratios. It is not a confidence interval. Mean and pooled approaches imply EV 362.5 and 372, or equity 277.5 and 287. The aggregation rule is a substantive choice about the comparison, not an interchangeable spreadsheet option.

Leaving each included firm out in turn gives medians 8, 6, 8 and 6. Four firms are a fragile comparison base. Report this sensitivity; do not silently delete P4 because its high price raises the result. A median reduces sensitivity to one extreme observation, but it cannot repair a shared accounting error, a poor peer universe or a sector-wide pricing mistake.

6. Use disagreement to identify an assumption to investigate

Morrow's synthetic quoted EV of 385 divided by its unadjusted peak subtotal 80 gives 4.8125×. Dividing by the matched normalized forward 50 gives 7.7×, 10% above the peer median of 7×. Neither number alone establishes mispricing. Applying the peers' forward multiple to the target's peak subtotal would produce EV 560 and equity 475, overstating the same-method normalized result by 210, or CU 21 per share. The error is a denominator mismatch, not a newly discovered source of value.

A second comparison uses EBIT. Peer forward EBIT is 48, 36, 45 and 60; the corresponding multiples are 7.5, 13⅓, 6⅔ and 12. The median is 9.75×. Applying it to target EBIT 40 gives EV 390 and equity 305, or CU 30.5 per share. EBITDA's 350 and EBIT's 390 differ because the peers' depreciation fractions differ and the two median constructions weight economic differences differently. Inspect maintenance, asset age, lease treatment and reinvestment rather than choosing whichever answer is more attractive.

The supported stable DCF gave EV 400 and equity 315. Holding its FCFF1 = 24 and g = 3% fixed, the rate that would make EV equal the peer-median 350 is r = 0.03+24/350 = 69/700 ≈ 9.8571%. The synthetic market EV 385 corresponds to 711/7700 ≈ 9.2338%. These are conditional implied rates, not independent estimates of risk. The gap could instead reflect a different margin, return on reinvestment, competitive duration, forecast bias or relative market pricing.

A DCF whose terminal value is set by the same peer multiple is not an independent confirmation of that multiple. Likewise, peer forecasts and the target forecast may share the same optimistic demand assumption. Keep separate the operating evidence, the discount-rate evidence and the price evidence. An unexplained average of several estimates can conceal the disagreement; a useful reconciliation identifies the changed assumption and shows its value effect.

Transactions and control. A takeover price can include the value of feasible operating improvements, buyer-specific synergies, control rights, financing effects or bargaining, net of integration costs. Trading prices concern a different claim and information setting. A transaction's target revenue or EBITDA may also precede the announcement by many months. Reconstruct the exact consideration, assumed debt and other claims, cash retained or transferred, earn-outs and relevant earnings period. A fixed “control premium” applied to every public-company multiple has no basis in the operating economics alone.

Damodaran's discussion of controlling for differences considers qualitative, modified-multiple and regression approaches. A growth-adjusted multiple does not automatically control for risk or reinvestment efficiency; the justified-multiple formula is nonlinear. A regression needs adequate observations, economically motivated controls, measurement discipline, uncertainty and out-of-sample assessment. Its residual is a conditional pricing difference, not a causal proof of undervaluation. Four synthetic peers do not support a reliable many-variable fit.

Reproduce and challenge the comparison

Download the complete fictional input register, standard-library benchmark, preserved exact output and experiment guide. Keep them together and run python3 v08-c07-analysis.py. The program uses exact rational arithmetic, prints JSON and makes no network request or file overwrite. It retains excluded candidates and their reasons, reproduces every normalization and claim bridge, distinguishes the three aggregates, checks leave-one-out sensitivity, and connects target ratios to the conditional DCF.

Its evidence flags are supplied teaching assumptions, not automated verification of economic comparability. Experiments should change the supporting narrative as well as a numerical input. An unsupported addback does not become defensible because the code accepts a rational number. The chapter supplies the interpretation; the lab makes the consequences inspectable.

Exercises

All amounts are fictional kCU unless specified. Values are at T0, after distributions; forward earnings cover the next twelve months. Use exact intermediate values and explain the claim, period or economic condition behind each calculation.

  1. A firm has ordinary equity 180, financial debt 50, leases 20, preference claims 10, NCI 15, excess cash 12 and an excluded holding 8. Recurring forward EBITDA is 35 after lease expense 5. Find capitalized-lease operating EV and its matched EBITDA multiple. If a supported comparable multiple of 7× is applied on that basis, find implied ordinary equity. Explain why NCI is added even though it does not belong to the parent.
  2. A supplied reported operating subtotal of 42 is after lease expense 6. It includes a genuinely isolated cost 5 and disposal gain 3, both settled before T0. Recurring warranty 4 and stock compensation 2 are also included; no economic case supports removing them. The Y1 cycle adjustment is −8 and a funded capacity addition contributes +6. Find normalized forward EBITDA and EBIT if D&A is 8. At EV 288, find the forward EBITDA multiple. Quantify the valuation error at that same multiple if management also removes the recurring warranty and compensation expenses.
  3. A stable business has first EBITDA 80, D&A 20, tax 20%, sales 400 and r = 10%. R is 16% and g is 4%. Find NOPAT, reinvestment, FCFF, EV and the justified EBITDA, EBIT and sales multiples. Increase g to 6% while holding first earnings and R fixed. Repeat the two growth choices for a separate business with R = 8% and the same first earnings. Explain the opposite growth effects and why the two R cases have different opening capital.
  4. Three eligible peers have (EV, forward EBITDA) of (120,20), (400,50) and (990,90). Find individual ratios, their median, arithmetic mean and pooled ratio. A target has forward EBITDA 30, net claims to subtract 40 and 12 thousand shares. Find its equity and per-share estimates under the median and pooled methods. State the pooled weights.
  5. For an explicitly supplied complete fictional cycle with equal weight per year, revenue is 100, 200 and 400, while consistently measured EBITDA is 10, 40 and 40. Next-period comparable revenue is 450. Estimate normal EBITDA using the equal-year average margin, then compare the result with the average dollar EBITDA and with the pooled historical margin. Explain the scaling and weighting differences. State what extra forecast is needed if normalization takes two years.
  6. Use the main six-candidate register. An analyst proposes to include P5's 4×, discard P4's 9× because it is “too expensive,” and rank P6's negative ratio as the cheapest. Compute the median from adding P5 to P1–P4 and the median from dropping P4 alone. Evaluate all three proposed changes. Specify the evidence and disclosure needed for a defensible change to the original peer rule.
  7. A share trades at CU 18. Current ordinary shares are 12 thousand; trailing common net income is 24 and weighted-average shares for that income are 10 thousand. Compute market capitalization/net income and price/reported trailing EPS. Explain why they differ. Next-year common income is expected to be 30 with 12 thousand shares throughout; compute forward EPS and P/E. Show what a two-for-one split does to the trailing price/EPS ratio when both price and historical EPS are adjusted.
  8. Start with Morrow's supported DCF of 400. An additional fully cash, after-tax transition expense of 12 occurs only in Y1; investment and all cash from Y2 onward stay unchanged. Value the revised cash path at 9%, showing the date-1 continuation. A separate transaction quotes operating EV 480, with estimated synergy PV 90 and integration-cost PV 20. Under the explicit decomposition assumption that the price includes all net synergies, find its implied standalone component. Explain why these figures and the peer-median 350 should prompt an assumption reconciliation, and why the transaction alone does not identify an unconditional standalone value.
Complete exercise solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. EV = 180+50+20+10+15−12−8 = 255. Matched EBITDA is 35+5 = 40, giving 51/8 = 6.375×. At 7×, operating value is 280. Net excluded claims are 50+20+10+15−12−8 = 75, so implied ordinary equity is 205. NCI is added because the denominator contains all consolidated subsidiary earnings, including the portion supporting outside owners; it is removed when returning to the parent's ordinary equity.

  2. The recurring common-basis subtotal is 42+6+5−3 = 50. Forward EBITDA is 50−8+6 = 48; EBIT is 40; EV/EBITDA is 6×. Unsupported removal of the recurring 4+2 produces EBITDA 54 and value 324, an overstatement of 36. The cash settlement of the isolated item does not authorize removing every recurring cost. No full tax or equity bridge was requested; this is a pre-tax operating-multiple comparison.

  3. EBIT is 60, NOPAT 48. At R = 16%, g = 4%, reinvestment is 48×0.04/0.16 = 12; FCFF 36; EV 600. Multiples are 7.5× EBITDA, 10× EBIT and 1.5× sales. At g = 6%, investment is 18, FCFF 30, EV 750 and EBITDA multiple 9.375×. At R = 8%, the 4% growth case invests 24, distributes 24 and is worth 400, or 5× EBITDA. The 6% case invests 36, distributes 12 and is worth 300, or 3.75×. Growth creates value at R > r and destroys it at R < r. Opening capital is 48/0.16 = 300 versus 48/0.08 = 600; within each R case, the growth comparison holds this base and first earnings fixed.

  4. Ratios are 6, 8 and 11. Median is 8, mean 25/3 ≈ 8.3333, and pooled ratio is (120+400+990)/(20+50+90) = 151/16 = 9.4375. Pooled weights are 1/8, 5/16 and 9/16. Under the median, target EV is 240, equity 200 and price CU 50/3 ≈ 16.6667. Under the pooled method, EV is 2265/8 = 283.125, equity 1945/8 = 243.125 and price CU 1945/96 ≈ 20.2604. Larger denominators receive larger pooled weights; calling that result the ordinary mean obscures its construction.

  5. Annual margins are 10%, 20%, 10%; their equal-year mean is 2/15 = 13⅓%. Applying it to revenue 450 gives normal EBITDA 60. Average dollar EBITDA is (10+40+40)/3 = 30; it retains the smaller historical scale. The pooled margin is 90/700 = 9/70, producing 405/7 ≈ 57.8571. It weights years by revenue rather than equally. None of these weighting choices proves what next year will earn; the prompt specifies the equal-year cycle rule. A two-year recovery requires explicit interim revenue, margins, investment and cash, then a dated continuing regime. A normalized denominator alone does not replace those transition cash flows.

  6. Adding P5 gives sorted ratios 4, 6, 6, 8, 9 and median 6×. Dropping P4 alone leaves 6, 6, 8 and median 6×. Both changes lower the result, but the direction is not a selection criterion. P5 could be informative only if its different risk, growth, margins and capital economics are credibly reconciled to the target; its 4× price is insufficient. P4's 9× can be retained and investigated unless a supported data/perimeter or economic-comparability reason warrants exclusion. P6's negative denominator cannot be ordered as a meaningful positive-profit multiple; its loss and distress remain important evidence. A complete answer states a revised economic rule independent of the desired value, applies it to every candidate, records rejected firms and data limitations, reconciles periods/claims, and presents results under both the original and revised rules. A higher regression fit or a narrower value range alone does not validate a change.

  7. Market capitalization is 18×12 = 216; capitalization/net income is 9×. Reported trailing EPS is 24/10 = CU 2.4, so price/EPS is 7.5×. One calculation uses current shares, the other the smaller historical weighted-average share count. Their equivalence requires matched share bases; neither arithmetic identity demonstrates different underlying operating value. Forward EPS is 30/12 = CU 2.5 and forward P/E 7.2×. A two-for-one split gives price 9 and split-adjusted trailing EPS 1.2; their ratio remains 7.5×. Current shares become 24 thousand and market capitalization stays 216.

  8. The expense lowers F1 from 24 to 12. Unchanged F2 is 24.72; its onward growth is 3%. TV1 = 24.72/0.06 = 412, so revised EV is (12+412)/1.09 = 42400/109 ≈ 388.990826, also 400−12/1.09. Continuing value is not reduced for an expense that ends in Y1. Under the stipulated full-synergy price decomposition, the transaction's standalone component is 480−90+20 = 410. Negotiation need not transfer all net synergy to the seller, and the synergy estimate itself may be wrong; without that decomposition assumption, standalone value is not identified by the quote. A complete reconciliation names which earnings/transition, reinvestment, risk, market-pricing and control assumptions differ; keeps claim dates and perimeters matched; quantifies at least the 12/1.09 expense effect; and proposes evidence to resolve the differences. A mechanical average of 350, 388.990826 and 410 supplies no such explanation.

Teach-back

Explain to a committee why Morrow's “4.8× versus peers at 7×” claim is incomplete. Use one price/claim reconciliation, one earnings reconciliation, the role of the excluded candidates, and one reason that the DCF differs from the peer-median result.

Illustrative teaching answer

Today's synthetic equity 300 becomes operating EV 385 only after adding debt, leases and outside equity and subtracting excluded cash/holdings. Its reported 80 includes gain 10 and peak contribution 20; the matched Y1 denominator is 50, making its ratio 7.7×. The four included peers give 7× only under a specified positive-profit manufacturing rule; software P5 and distressed P6 remain visible with reasons and downside information. The cash-supported DCF yields 8× because its taxes, reinvestment and 9% rate imply FCFF 24 and value 400. A 9.8571% rate would reconcile the same cash with 350, but different cash economics could also explain the difference. The next evidence request should identify a disputed operating or risk assumption, not ask for a more favorable peer list.

Delayed check

After 7–14 days, answer without the examples. (1) EV is 200, peak earnings 50 and matched normal earnings 25. Find both multiples. (2) EV 280 supports financial debt 60, leases 15 and NCI 5; excess cash is 10, with no other claim or excluded asset. Find ordinary-equity value and price for 7 thousand shares. (3) First EBITDA is 40, D&A fraction 25%, tax 20%, R = 12%, g = 3% and r = 9%. Find supported FCFF and EV/EBITDA. (4) Peers trade at 5×, 5× and 20×. Find median and mean, and state whether the high ratio alone authorizes exclusion.

Delayed-check answers

(1) 4× on peak earnings and 8× on normal earnings. (2) Equity is 280−60−15−5+10 = 210; price CU 30. (3) EBIT 30 gives NOPAT 24; b = 25%, investment 6 and FCFF 18. EV is 300 and its EBITDA multiple 7.5×. (4) Median 5×, mean 10×. The high ratio requires an evidence-based data or comparability investigation; discarding it solely for being high biases the chosen comparison.

Sources, limits and next step

The scoped primary sources are the definition and analytical tests for multiples, the claim/perimeter definitions, earnings normalization and timing, methods for controlling differences, and the cited U.S. SEC staff interpretations. All prices, forecasts, business cases, exercises and code are original fictional teaching inputs. No source company example or historical market statistic is presented as a current observation.

The small register establishes arithmetic and interpretive discipline, not empirical peer selection or an estimate of a real company's fair price. Diligence still requires the actual claims, business evidence and forecast uncertainty. The next chapter's contingent investment choices add a further comparability question: two firms with similar current earnings may hold very different rights to expand, wait or abandon.

Sources and further study

  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — The Anatomy of a Multiple — Claim and accounting consistency, explicit multiple definitions, peer-universe and outlier questions, and the connection between multiples and cash-flow fundamentals.
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — Financial Measures and Ratios: enterprise-value definitions — Operating EV, market versus book claims, consolidated noncontrolling interests, excluded holdings and consistent operating denominators.
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — More on Normalizing Earnings — Scale-adjusted versus dollar earnings normalization and the importance of when recovery occurs.
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — Controlling for Differences across Firms — Qualitative adjustments, modified multiples and regression as alternative ways to investigate differences in growth, risk and cash-flow economics.
  • U.S. SEC Division of Corporation Finance — Non-GAAP Financial Measures, scoped staff interpretations — Dated U.S. disclosure reference for recurring-cost exclusions, consistency and symmetry, adjusted measure labels and net-income reconciliation; not universal accounting law.
